data.content_ref: inline:The isolated artifact inherits the covering principle from SRC_005 but extends it from a binary decorrelation criterion to a graduated spectrum: causal decorrelation is not a threshold property but admits degrees measured by the verdict's sensitivity to perturbations of increasing semantic distance from the original claim. A perturbation of count±1 (SCR_002) tests shallow decorrelation; an injected false claim with a different semantic structure (SRC_003) tests deeper decorrelation; a cross-engine check with independent training (SRC_004) tests the deepest level. The covering principle thus abstracts to a family of perturbation tests indexed by semantic distance, and genuine independence is the limit as semantic distance approaches zero while verdict sensitivity remains nonzero. This inherits SRC_005's core insight but contradicts SRC_003's claim that single-run procedural evidence is insufficient — because on this spectrum, a single high-sensitivity perturbation at shallow semantic distance can match the diagnostic power of a population of trials at greater distances. This is REFUTED IF the perturbation-sensitivity curve is shown to be flat — i.e., verdict sensitivity does not increase with semantic perturbation distance — which would collapse the spectrum into a binary property and eliminate the graduated structure.
